record.paper_title: On Open Problems in Biological Network Visualization
record.original_question: Given a biological network whose nodes or edges carry multiple attributes, including time-series data for studying dynamic biological behavior and mixtures of nominal, ordinal, scalar, categorized spatial, and uncertain data, how can one design a visual representation that lets investigators understand co-regulated elements and their connections within the network at large scale? The solution should find a readable combination of visual encodings for different data types and should determine when to use integrated node or edge encodings, preattentive visual features, or coordinated multiple views, while avoiding the failure mode in which small embedded graphics become too difficult to compare in a large graph and avoiding excessive spatial separation or cross-view linking burden.

evidence.quote: The data belongs to different data types, namely: nominal data such as sequence names or categories; ordinal data such as ontologies, rankings, or partly ordered information; scalar data such as comparisons or ratios; categorized spatial data
The challenge here lies in finding a harmonic combination of visual representations for mixtures of different data types.

simple use of small visualizations that replace, for example, the node representations is most of the time not sufficient, as a visual comparison of such small graphics in a large graph becomes very quickly infeasible.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E) be a large graph (intended to model a biological network) in which every vertex v ∈ V and every edge e ∈ E is decorated with a tuple of attributes drawn from heterogeneous data types, including: (i) nominal attributes (e.g. labels or categories), (ii) ordinal attributes (e.g. rankings or partial orders coming from ontologies), (iii) scalar attributes (real-valued measurements, ratios, or comparisons), (iv) categorized spatial attributes (locations or regions belonging to a finite set of categories), (v) time-series attributes (functions t ↦ x_v(t) or t ↦ x_e(t) sampled at finitely many time points), and (vi) uncertain attributes (values equipped with probability distributions or error intervals).

Design a visual encoding scheme Φ that maps G together with all of its attributes to a planar layout with associated graphical marks, satisfying the following requirements:

1. Φ chooses, for each attribute type listed above, a visual channel (e.g. hue, luminance, shape, size, orientation, texture, position) or composite glyph, and specifies whether the channel is attached to the node mark, to the edge mark, or to a coordinated auxiliary view.

2. Φ enables a viewer to identify, at the scale of the entire graph, sets of co-regulated elements — i.e. groups of nodes or edges whose time-series and scalar attributes are correlated above a chosen threshold — together with the topological connections among them.

3. Φ uses preattentive visual features (features detectable in less than ~250 ms without serial search) for the comparisons that must be performed across the whole graph.

4. Φ avoids the failure mode in which small per-node embedded graphics (e.g. miniature time-series plots) become too small to be visually compared in a large graph, and simultaneously avoids the opposite failure mode in which information is split across so many coordinated views that the cross-view linking cost dominates.

Provide such a scheme Φ together with a precise specification of which visual channels are assigned to which attribute types, when integrated node/edge encodings are used versus coordinated multiple views, and a justification (theoretical or empirical) that the resulting representation simultaneously meets requirements (1)–(4).
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broadly stated design challenge for visualizing multi-attribute biological networks. No definitive general solution has been reported; the visualization research community treats it as an ongoing open problem, with partial solutions (glyph-based encodings, small multiples, linked views) addressing restricted attribute subsets but no unified scheme meeting all stated requirements.
